GRU gate saturation alone does not establish lost temporal credit. Saturated gates can preserve state while becoming difficult to learn; diagnose the full recurrent Jacobian and target-score gradients across interaction lags. Under PyTorch’s convention, hₜ=(1−zₜ)nₜ+zₜhₜ₋₁, so z near one preserves the direct state path. Gate statistics omit indirect derivatives through gates and candidate states. Foundational evidence: [Improving the Gating Mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09890); implementation convention: [PyTorch GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html).

Recent attribution research supports triangulation. The 2024 [Sanity Checks Revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06465) examines weaknesses of parameter-randomization tests; explanation changes after randomization are insufficient evidence of faithfulness. A 2025 [time-series perturbation study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-09538-2) finds evaluation depends strongly on perturbation method and region size. These are general methodological findings, not direct GRU4Rec mechanism validation.

Suggested application to the existing checkpoint: verify instrumented recurrence reproduces original outputs; confirm left-padding leaves state unchanged and readout selects the final nonpadding position. Measure gate saturation, lag-wise embedding gradients, and target-directed Jacobian-vector products on real interactions. Compare attribution ordering against equal-length item replacements or swaps, preserving padding and using random/low-attribution controls. Report hidden-state displacement separately from target-score change, target-versus-candidate margins, and rank changes on fixed candidates: state movement need not affect ranking. Require agreement across gradients and interventions before interpreting a mechanism; these are proposed diagnostic checks, not measured findings.
